pos.text: I know this game is hated as an mmo. In fact I didn't even know this game existed until it ended up on the Worst MMO Ever series on YouTube. I actually fell in love with it BECAUSE of that video. To paraphrase Josh, it's not an MMO, it's a solo rpg being played alongside others. It's cozy and soothing. This game is like Albion with no PVP and it scratches the same itch in my brain as Stardew Valley. I'm planning to try and max it. I've never done it in a grind game and for some reason I love this one. It's simple. I've thought of getting into other super grindy MMO's before but they always end up overwhelming me. This game is simplistic and easy to learn. The maps are basic, enemies are a slug match with little to no mechs, gear is RNGezus until Act 4. The grind is intense. At 24 hours I'm 23 combat, 47 foraging, 35 fishing; this is as someone who only works part time. I'm also obviously

Look, I'll be straight with you. Brighter Shores is weird. It's from Andrew Gower, one of the original RuneScape creators, and it really shows. This is an MMO that knows exactly what it wants to be, which is both its biggest strength and its most glaring weakness.

~~The World Actually Has Personality

Right off the bat, you're a town guard in Hopeport, and honestly? The writing has this dry British humor that just works. There's a storm messing with the harbor, goblins are causing trouble, and you gradually discover you're destined to become a Cryoknight, Guardian, or Hammermage. It's not Shakespeare, but it's charming as hell. The game has this cozy vibe that makes you want to keep clicking around just to see what quirky dialogue pops up next.

The 18 professions are where things get interesting. You can fish, forage, cook, mine, blacksmith, brew potions. There's a ton to dig int
I dont know why but every time I play this game, I get on so excited to play, then 5 minutes later I start dozing off. I call the game Sleepy Shores when I talk about it now.

Came here from Josh Strife Hayes both critical and poignant review of Brighter Shores. After listening, laughing, and perusing my way through his critics of Andrew Gower's newest masterpiece, I jokingly did what many of us millennial gamers do, and decided to play Brighter Shores "For the Lolz". 

Immediately upon entering the game and working through the tutorial I could see all of the critics Josh Strife Hayes pointed out in full form. The simple combat, the silly quest dialogue the pedantic progression. I never played much of OSRS so I had no way to compare the two on an objective level but had enough exposure to the game through YT and streamers to know the similarities were there. 

However this is where the deviation began. A friend of mine jumped into the game with me to play, we added each other as friends and quickly realized, "Wait we cant group up or quest together." No ma
I truly believe this game will become something great in the future, and I plan to stay till then.

I played this game on day of release. There was so much to do in the short term and I loved some of the story. It was a little clunky during that time but it's smoothed out now.

Pros:
- Many skills to train from 1-500.
- 3 Different combat classes.
- A good list of quests to complete.
- Cool capes to unlock as you level and holiday vanity items.
- You can play as a lone wolf (ironman) or as a regular account.
- You can train skills while offline.

Cons:
- Updates may not come in order of announcement.
- As of time of this review, there are no repeatable bosses with their own drops.
- As of time of this review there are no special attacks.
- As of time of this review the player count has dipped a ton.

Conclusion:
I would still recommend this game even if there were 0 players active. You don't need others to feel like you've accomplished something in-game. I have had fun with what's avai

First off, I have not played Runescape. Yes, I know everyone just says this is Runescape, but I have 0 nostalgia for it so my opinion on this game is based off Brighter Shores and only it.

I have really been enjoying this. Yes, it is a grind game. You go and grind combat, grind foraging, grind fishing, grind cooking, grind potion making, and probably grind whatever other professions I haven't seen yet. So you need to be okay mindlessly doing an action. This is just a VERY casual game. Even combat is just click enemy and start combat. Maybe activate a heal potion if you are dying faster than the enemy. Think of it like a "2nd monitor game" as I've seen people put it. So if you are looking for a game to have running in the background while doing other things or just relax to, give it a try.

Definitely check it out. Brighter Shores and its interface handles incredibly well at any window size with a style and music that are very dialed in. If you like incremental games, ironman in Runescape, or a "point-and-click style RPG" (notice the lack of MMO in that statement), I think it's superb. 

The decision-making in the game as to how you're going about the grinds feels significant, but open to preference and there are catch up mechanics in the form of "knowledge" rewards and offline passive training. Being reductionist, everything's "the same", but there are intentional vibe changes across the professions based on the room designs, interaction timings, and how they scale into further progression. If you look for the quirks, you can get a little creative with how you're picking and choosing the nodes and seek out better rates, which involves more observation and strategy. Tricks
this is not a game, this is a busywork simulator. it's probably not what you're looking for, but it's exactly what i was looking for.

Brighter Shores is a charming and cozy adventure that immediately gave me nostalgic RuneScape Classic vibes, just with a fresh coat of modern graphics and polish. The art style is cute, inviting, and relaxing, making it an easy game to sink into for long stretches without feeling overwhelmed.

That said, the overall gameplay structure leans heavily toward slow, grind-based progression. Skills must be repeated over and over to level up, which can feel meditative at times but undeniably repetitive. If you enjoy incremental advancement and classic skilling loops, this won’t bother you, but players expecting fast rewards or constant variety may find the pacing sluggish.

Even though other players appear in the world, Brighter Shores currently feels very much like a single-player experience. In the many hours I’ve played, not a single message has appeared in chat, and I haven’t seen anyone el

I really enjoy this game personally. I see a lot of haters comparing it to runescape, and I don't see the point? This is in early access.. Runescape is a fully released game. It obviously doesn't have as much content yet, but it is getting there.
The devs are working hard and adding new things all the time. Stop comparing it to a fully released game, and enjoy the game for what it is, a funny little grind game that you get to see build up itself from the very beginning.

I like it as a grind game. 
It feel's as if the 'grind' part of a grindy game, has been optimized for enjoyment.  ( Probably from RuneScape data :P , but that's a win! )

The learning curve is not very intuitive, but there is a pretty good selection of information on the Brighter Shores Wiki. Eventually, with a little brainpower you can figure out what's going on and the game's flow.

I enjoy the idea of each 'Main-area' as a fully playable zone all in its own. The skills are distinct, and serve a purpose of serving other skills. The cross skill interaction is well-thought out, and I can imagine that future refinements to cross skill cohesion even better. This really shows through with the unlocking of the Mines.

 I also enjoy that the method's of training is both primary skill with the bonus of Skill Point Experience. This is the incentive to play the game actively. -I hear it's
It's a fun casual game. Great if you only able to play a game for 1-2 hrs a day. You can do passive play which helps get the levels up. This is perfect for busy work life schedule.

It's fun if youre looking for a side mmo. Like something you grind while doing other stuff. Its def a grind. If anyone is coming from Runescape (I thankfully was privileged enough as a kid to pass over runescape for things like everquest) dont take their opinion too seriously, give it a go and try it for yourself.

I'm only about 20-25 hours into this game but I think it's way overhated. Seriously, people talk about this game like it threw their grandmother down a flight of stairs and used their cat as a silencer, Postal-style. I never got into Runescape and it's a very intimidating game for a newcomer and I think Brighter Shores has a good onboarding process. Controlling the camera with the mouse instead of the arrow keys like Runescape is another welcome quality of life update. Seriously, put your right hand on the mouse and left hand on the arrow keys and you'll know how awkward that is. The game is grindy, yes, but I don't think it's that much different than another grindy game I've actually played like Albion Online.  Combat is basic but functional, hopefully upcoming changes help it out.

The monetization is also fair in that you pay for content and not for easier grind or for power. Hell, XP
Excellent game for just starting out. I look forward to many updates to this.

Runescape today feels like a mockery of what we knew it to be growing up. Bonds, massive exp farms, easy gains, inflated economy, the list goes on.

As someone who has played since 2001 the game today feels like it's been taken away from me in away. It's nearly impossible to get into anymore as a true oldschool player not whatever the hell OSRS is now.

The creator of runescape that we knew left, Andrew sold the game and it became fortnite like. Andrew went on to make a new game called Brighter Shores on steam.

Brighter shores plays exactly like how RuneScape did for the first 8 years. And as veteran of runescape, I find it more enjoyable to play over RS in 2026.

TL;DR: Runescape 2026 is for Gen Z and Brighter Shores is for Millennials who played classic 2001 rs
I've been enjoying the quest, the skills levelings, the interaction with community.

What I've found in all my playtime is the most relaxing version of progression for this style of RPG than I've found elsewhere. I can't play it as much as I'd like anymore but I'll probably always jump back in from time to time. That's a game you can keep in your back pocket, and it's worth it at that price if you want to explore past the free content.

Brighter Shores is a wonderful reimagining of the classic RSlike rpg game. It is clear that it is well thought out and improves on many of the weak points of the other game. Brighter Shores is by no means perfect and is improving from ongoing development.
Nice and relaxing. Pretty simple, but perfect when you're in the mood for something not too taxing. Music is awesome!

a good grindy rpg. I cant wait till the multiplayer stuff starts. maybe being able to party and share exp or trade items to help lvl cooking or alchemy while your friend makes all your gear. fingers crossed this keeps going.

I decided to leave a review after a year and a measly twenty hours, I've started to get into the game and I am absolutely enjoying it, the progression feels really nice and smooth, the dialogue is in line with Andrew Gower's other work (I love it), I'm not a fan of the art style but that won't stop me from playing and enjoying the game. Andrew made my childhood and gave me many memories with his other game and this new game of his will leave me with some as well. I should add that there's a few complaints from a group of people who rag on the game due to there being holiday events along with cool, event only items, I'll say this, if you think missing an item in an MMO is bad then this genre is not for you, I don't mean any disrespect but I believe if you desire to have every single item in a game then you are better off playing non-RPG, single player games.

There should always be exclus

It is a simple and straight forward game, while I hope one day for a touch interface for my wrists, I would say Gower is succeeding in making a delightful experience. Along with the (currently at least) reasonable fee for membership I would say it is a worthwhile game.

I personally really enjoy this game. You can tell it is technically very well made, as it runs well on basically any PC. It also looks great, in my opinion, due to the nice art style.

I realise that the game misses some more dynamic content, but I personally always enjoyed the basic skill grinding in Runescape/OSRS, and the grinding in this game appeals to me as well. Usually I listen to music or do other stuff on my PC while playing, while slowly making progress.

Give it a go if you think you might be interested! I hope the game survives despite the current negative opinions.

Brighter Shores is a tedious, clunky chore simulator masquerading as nostalgia. The rigid room-by-room grid movement makes exploration feel incredibly claustrophobic, and the gameplay is nothing but an endless, mind-numbing point-and-click grind. It is so inherently boring that its main selling point is letting you progress while offline, which is a blatant admission that the game isn't actually fun to play. Once you hit the premium paywall for later zones, there is absolutely no reason to keep clicking.

Brighter Shores offers great humour and a delightful art style, giving it a lot of personality. That said, the skills never quite feel enjoyable enough to keep you hooked, and the game doesn’t offer the same sense of community or social connection you’d expect from most MMORPGs. It’s charming, but it feels like something is missing.

Brighter Shores starts strong, but once the initial excitement fades, it quickly reveals itself to be more of an idle progression game than a true MMO. After the early hours, gameplay largely devolves into logging in to update passive skills, with little reason to stay online or interact with other players. Outside of temporary events, the world feels empty, and the lack of meaningful multiplayer systems makes long-term engagement difficult.

When the game first launched, it genuinely felt promising. Progression was engaging, systems felt fresh, and there was a sense that the world would eventually open up into something deeper. Those early hours set expectations for an MMO experience that rewards time, investment, and community involvement.

So, I've been following videos and updates on this game for a while, as well as observing the playerbase. Decided to give it a try anyway, being a RS veteran like the rest of you (mostly) I'd imagine. I created a character, some good customization options right off the bat, designed a character I liked, went to name my character aaaannndd.... Paywall! As a F2p player, I was forced to have "#1" after my selected name (ex. HeroName#1) If I was p2p I wouldn't have to have the pesky pound sign and number after my lovely name. Played anyway. I enjoyed a bit of the dialogue in the tut quest, some cheeky lines and personality, and played till I could explore a bit. The exploration is very linear at first, I would imagine it opens more after the into quests, but this is what led me to putting the game down. I love long grindy games. I also don't mid the progression reset. What I do mind is that this game is lacking in any element of fun. Are you stuck cooking eel for hours on end to level cooking? You wanna know what makes that fun? The other people around also leveling cooking. However there is no one socializing, because there isn't ever a reason to. Even when there is a reason to it becomes impossible because the map sections are so small it's almost impossible.

MMO's live and die on their communities. This game could become an offline solo game and nothing would change.

This game is like if you took the grinding aspect of Runescape and took out everything else. It feels completely unrewarding and feels more like a menu sim where the ONLY thing you can do is grind skills. I know there's more, but you have to go so out of your way that it isn't fun anymore. 12 hours into this game only to get to a new area and... do the same grinding quests... 

Not fun.

The reason why this game is so divisive is simple: this is actually an incremental "idle game" disguised as a MMORPG.

Given that this obviously looks like RuneScape, most people expect quests, combat, a story and some exploration. There is basically none of that. As an example, there's an average of 5 quests per area (with 4 areas currently in the game).

What there is, however, is a bunch of skills that you can level up at a slow but constant rate without much effort, and a "passive activity" system where you keep gaining XP after logging out. So you come to the game every day, you watch number go up, that's it, that's the game.

To unlock the passive skills you have to do manual grinding, but the ratio is something like 1 day of actual gameplay for 1 week of doing nothing, so it really positions itself as a long-term background game.
